Crushed, they have gone into cosmetics, medicines and paint
Almost any shelled mollusc can make one, though most are mere curiosities

explanations: The most valuable are perfectly round and smooth; the many other shapes are known as baroque.
They have been crushed and used in cosmetics, medicines and paint formulations.
Almost all species of shelled mollusc can produce them, but most such concretions have no value except as curiosities.
The wild kind is extremely rare, and cultured or farmed ones from oysters and freshwater mussels make up most of those sold.
It is a hard, glistening object grown inside the soft tissue of a living shelled mollusc, of calcium carbonate laid down in concentric layers.

sources.excerpt: More commercially valuable pearls are perfectly round and smooth, but many other shapes, known as baroque pearls, can occur.
They have also been crushed and used in cosmetics, medicines, and paint formulations.
However, almost all species of shelled mollusks are capable of producing pearls (technically "calcareous concretions") of lesser shine or less spherical shape.

The most valuable pearls occur spontaneously in the wild but are extremely rare. These wild pearls are referred to as natural pearls. Cultured or farmed pearls from pearl oysters and freshwater mussels make up the majority of those currently sold.

Just like the shell of a mollusk, a pearl is composed of calcium carbonate (mainly aragonite or a mixture of aragonite and calcite) in minute crystalline form, which is deposited in concentric layers.
